metadata.note: The four routes that joined Kokomo's railroads to the rest of the network. kokomo_railroads.geojson drew three corridors through Kokomo -- Tipton-Peru, Frankfort-Marion and Kokomo-Logansport -- and said so in its own incomplete_coverage field: the Clover Leaf and Lake Erie and Western beyond Marion and Peru were 'outside the Kokomo area this layer covers'. The result was three lines that began and ended nowhere. This layer adds the missing ends. (1) South from Tipton to Indianapolis and (2) north from Peru to Michigan City complete the Peru & Indianapolis / Lake Erie and Western Indianapolis Division, about 161 miles end to end, reaching the Big Four and Pennsylvania lines at Indianapolis and the Michigan Central at Michigan City. (3) East from Marion through Delphos to Toledo carries the Clover Leaf back towards where it started -- a Delphos pharmacist's narrow gauge line -- and meets the Erie at Delphos and the New York Central at Toledo. (4) North-west from Logansport through Winamac, La Crosse and Valparaiso to Chicago is the Pennsylvania's Columbus-to-Chicago main line, which is what the Kokomo-Logansport trains connected to. Added 2026-08-27 in answer to the question of why Kokomo's lines were isolated. Colours and era boundaries follow kokomo_railroads.geojson so the new pieces and the old ones read as one railroad (CLAUDE.md Rule 4).
metadata.still_not_connected: The Clover Leaf WEST of Frankfort -- Veedersburg, Charleston, Illinois and on to East St. Louis, roughly 240 of the railroad's 450.72 miles -- is still not drawn. That is a whole railroad rather than a connecting link, and it was left out deliberately rather than overlooked. The Pennsylvania's Columbus-to-Chicago main line SOUTH-EAST of Logansport, through Anoka, Marion and Union City to Columbus, is likewise not drawn. Also still absent, as kokomo_railroads.geojson already records, is the Indianapolis-Logansport/Peru interurban of the Indiana Union Traction Company and the Indiana Railroad, which ran through Kokomo from 1903 to 1938: OSM carries almost no geometry for it.
metadata.not_yet_sourced: Every headway_min and avg_speed_kmh in this file is an estimate; no timetable was consulted for any of these lines. The Nickel Plate features here end in 1965, the system-wide end of Nickel Plate passenger service, for the same reason kokomo_railroads.geojson gives: no branch-specific discontinuance date was found, and local service on these Indiana lines, which faced heavy interurban competition, very likely ended well before that. Read 1965 as an upper bound. There is also a source conflict on when the Peru & Indianapolis reached Kokomo -- kokomo_railroads.geojson follows a source giving 1854, while the source used here gives Kokomo in 1853 and Peru in early 1854. Neither has been resolved; this layer does not draw Kokomo itself, so nothing here turns on it, but the conflict is recorded rather than silently decided.

properties.geometry_quality: Corridor-constrained trace over OpenStreetMap railway ways (rail, abandoned, disused and razed), routed leg by leg between the documented station towns: Indianapolis, Fishers, Noblesville, Cicero, Arcadia, Atlanta and Tipton. Each leg is a shortest path weighted to hug the corridor, with ways tagged to another historic operator penalised threefold, so the trace stays on this company's rails where OSM records who owned them. 11 legs in all; 6 routed on real mapped track and 5 drawn as STRAIGHT LINES totalling 22.0 km (4.06 km near [-86.14, 39.783]; 4.54 km near [-86.115, 39.814]; 4.05 km near [-86.09, 39.85]; 3.95 km near [-86.07, 39.883]; 5.40 km near [-86.05, 39.915]). Traced length 38.9 miles. The Peru & Indianapolis opened 21.42 miles to Noblesville in 1851 and reached Tipton in 1852; Indianapolis to Tipton is about 40 route miles, which the trace matches. THIS IS THE WEAKEST OF THE FOUR CONNECTIONS IN THIS LAYER and should be read with that in mind: every straight-line leg is between Indianapolis and Fishers, roughly a third of the drawn line, because the ex-Nickel Plate approach into downtown Indianapolis has been lifted and OpenStreetMap carries almost nothing for it. kokomo_railroads.geojson already recorded this hole in its incomplete_coverage field. North of Fishers, through Noblesville, Cicero, Arcadia and Atlanta to Tipton, every leg is on real mapped track, much of it the Nickel Plate Trail on the original right-of-way. 1 vertices that made the line double back on itself were trimmed afterwards -- the leg-by-leg routing overshoots a waypoint and comes back, which reads on the map as a spur that never existed; the repo's reversal and revisit spike tests both come back clean on the result. CAVEAT (CLAUDE.md Rule 2): this is the modern surviving alignment (active track in places, rail-trail and abandoned right-of-way in others) drawn back to the 19th century, and it has not been checked against a period valuation map.

segments.note: The southern end of the first railroad into Kokomo. The Peru & Indianapolis was incorporated on 19 January 1846 to link Indianapolis with the Wabash and Erie Canal at Peru; construction began at Indianapolis in 1849 and service opened over 21.42 miles to Noblesville on 12 March 1851, reaching Tipton in 1852 and going on to Kokomo and Peru. This feature is drawn from 1852, the year the rails reached Tipton, so that the drawn years do not assert service over track that was not yet there. The company was renamed the Indianapolis, Peru & Chicago on 11 March 1864; that renaming is not drawn as a separate era here, to stay consistent with the Tipton-Peru feature in kokomo_railroads.geojson, which also runs the Peru & Indianapolis name to 1887. headway_min is an estimate, not read off a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the 19 January 1846 incorporation, the 1849 start of construction, the 21.42 miles to Noblesville on 12 March 1851, the 1852 arrival at Tipton and the 11 March 1864 renaming are carried by the references below; the headway is NOT sourced.

segments.note: Foreclosure brought the Indianapolis, Peru & Chicago into the Lake Erie and Western on 8 April 1887, making this the southern end of the LE&W's Indianapolis Division and putting Indianapolis on a 718-mile system. Passenger business on the division fell away after 1900 under competition from the parallel interurban, and by the 1910s passenger revenue was a minor part of the railroad's traffic. headway_min is an estimate, not read off a timetable.

segments.note: The northern half of the line, and a different set of builders from the Peru & Indianapolis south of Peru. The Cincinnati, Peru & Chicago, created 23 June 1853, built Plymouth to La Porte in 1855; the Michigan City and Indianapolis Railroad, chartered by the state on 4 June 1870, connected La Porte to Michigan City from 1871. Those roads were consolidated as the Chicago, Cincinnati & Louisville, and in 1871 the Indianapolis, Peru & Chicago -- the renamed Peru & Indianapolis -- took over its 88 miles between Peru and Michigan City, completing a through Indianapolis-to-Michigan City railroad of about 161 miles. headway_min is an estimate, not read off a timetable.

segments.note: East from Marion towards where the Clover Leaf actually began. The Toledo, Cincinnati and St. Louis Railroad was formed in February 1881 out of several 3-foot narrow gauge lines, one of them the road a Delphos, Ohio pharmacist named Joseph Hunt had started from Delphos to Toledo; 1881 is also the year the railroad reached Marion, at Fourth and McClure streets. The company reorganised in June 1886 as the Toledo, St. Louis and Kansas City and standard-gauged its line: on 26 June 1887 some 2,000 men and boys widened the whole 206 miles between Frankfort, Indiana and Toledo in eleven hours. It was renamed the Toledo, St. Louis and Western in 1900. This feature covers the Marion-Toledo end of a 450.72-mile Toledo-East St. Louis railroad. headway_min is an estimate, not read off a timetable.
sources: Segment-level: the February 1881 formation from narrow gauge lines, Joseph Hunt and the Delphos origin, the 1881 arrival at Marion, the June 1886 reorganisation, the 26 June 1887 standard-gauging of the 206 miles Frankfort-Toledo, the 1900 renaming and the 450.72-mile system length are carried by the references below; the headway is NOT sourced.

segments.note: What the Kokomo line connected to. The Chicago and Cincinnati Railroad opened Logansport west through La Crosse to Valparaiso in 1861, and the Chicago and Great Eastern Railway completed La Crosse to Chicago in 1865, absorbing the Chicago and Cincinnati later that year; by 1868 the whole Columbus-to-Chicago main line was in place under the Columbus, Chicago and Indiana Central, which passed to the Pennsylvania Railroad. Trains off the Kokomo line joined it at Logansport, and the route also carried the Pennsylvania's Chicago-Cincinnati and Chicago-Louisville passenger trains. headway_min of 240 stands for several trains each way per day and is an estimate, not read off a timetable.

segments.note: The Pennsylvania and the New York Central merged into Penn Central on 1 February 1968, and Penn Central ran this line's passenger trains until Amtrak took over on 1 May 1971. Amtrak did drop and then restore service over the route -- the ex-New York Central line between Kankakee and Cincinnati was in too poor a state for respectable speeds -- and the last passenger train here was Amtrak's Floridian in 1975. That Amtrak era is NOT drawn in this feature, which ends where Penn Central operation ends. headway_min is an estimate, not read off a timetable.
